headline: High: LightAgent’s broad network/MCP/tooling can amplify prompt-injection, leakage, and cascading-action risks when paired with a prompt repository that may supply untrusted instructions.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: awesome-prompts is a prompt repository, so its content can be treated as instruction-like input; LightAgent exposes MCP/stdin-stdout and browser/tool execution, which can ingest and act on such content. The pairwise bridge is plausible but not directly documented, so I choose medium rather than low because the interaction exists in default-style workflows and uncertainty escalates.
conditions: IF LightAgent reads prompts or files sourced from awesome-prompts without provenance checks, injection is possible.
IF the pair is connected through MCP/stdin-stdout or copied prompt text, attacker-controlled instructions can traverse the boundary.
mitigations: Require provenance labels on imported prompts.
Render repository content as data, not instructions.
Disable automatic execution of copied prompt templates.
Add a manual review step before any prompt is fed into LightAgent.
requires-engineering: add content-sanitization and provenance tracking in the orchestrator.

B_data_leakage.rationale: awesome-prompts itself shows no data classes touched and no egress, but LightAgent touches conversations, memory, trace data, tool results, and has broad network egress. If any sensitive prompt or workspace content from the pair enters LightAgent, it can be transmitted outward. The evidence is indirect, so medium fits better than low because leakage can affect multiple work products.
conditions: IF prompt text or files from awesome-prompts contain secrets or internal data, LightAgent may exfiltrate them via network egress.
IF LightAgent is configured with external APIs, its context window can leave the local boundary.
mitigations: Keep sensitive prompts out of shared workspaces.
Restrict LightAgent egress to allowlisted endpoints.
Strip secrets before passing content between agents.
Review logs for accidental prompt capture.
requires-engineering: enforce redaction before outbound tool/API calls.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: awesome-prompts has no write, network, or runtime surfaces, while LightAgent can spawn subprocesses and use MCP. There is no documented shared mutable resource or overlapping write scope, so direct capability conflict is limited. I keep this low because the pair lacks a clear same-target write path, though uncertainty remains.
conditions: IF both agents are pointed at the same mutable external resource through MCP or subprocesses, conflicts can emerge.
IF an orchestrator adds a shared writable workspace, write contention becomes possible.
mitigations: Assign separate working directories.
Serialize any shared-resource writes.
Disable unnecessary subprocess spawning.
Use per-agent credentials for external services.
requires-engineering: add locking around shared mutable resources.

D_cascading_error.rationale: awesome-prompts can supply prompt content that LightAgent may treat as authoritative input, and LightAgent has tool-calling plus browser/MCP capabilities that can turn that input into downstream actions. There is no direct evidence of a specific workflow, so I do not rate high, but the default-style path from prompt text to action is plausible and can propagate errors.
conditions: IF LightAgent consumes prompts from awesome-prompts without verification, incorrect instructions can cascade into tool calls.
IF downstream workflows trust LightAgent outputs as facts, errors can propagate to actions.
mitigations: Require human review before tool execution.
Add citation/grounding checks on generated claims.
Separate prompt ingestion from action execution.
Log and diff tool plans before execution.
requires-engineering: implement verification gates for downstream actions.

E_compliance.rationale: No explicit residency, certification, or retention mismatch is documented for awesome-prompts, and LightAgent’s docs only show broad data handling and secret types. Because compliance risk is not evidenced as a concrete mismatch, I keep this low; the other agent is not cited beyond its lack of sensitive data classes because it appears content-only.
conditions: IF LightAgent processes regulated data classes through its external APIs, compliance obligations may change.
IF repository content is repurposed to include regulated data, retention and logging controls become relevant.
mitigations: Avoid regulated data in prompts.
Confirm retention settings for LightAgent logs.
Review secret-handling paths.
Document data-flow boundaries.
requires-engineering: add residency and retention controls.
